description.summary: Cadborosaurus, popularly 'Caddy', is a sea-serpent cryptid reported along the Pacific coast from Alaska to California, with the densest cluster of sightings in the inland waters around Vancouver Island, British Columbia, and named after Cadboro Bay near Victoria.
description.full: Cadborosaurus, commonly called 'Caddy', is a marine cryptid associated with the inland and coastal waters of the Pacific Northwest, particularly the Strait of Georgia, Cadboro Bay, and the waters around Vancouver Island. Witnesses describe a long-necked, serpentine animal with a horse- or camel-like head, vertical humps or coils behind the head, and either flippers or a fan-shaped tail; reported lengths range from approximately 5 m (15 ft) to over 30 m (100 ft) in the most extravagant accounts. The modern phenomenon coalesced in the autumn of 1933, when Major W. H. Langley, clerk of the British Columbia Legislature, reported a sighting from his sailboat near Discovery Island, off Cadboro Bay; the Victoria Daily Times' managing editor Archie Wills coined the name 'Cadborosaurus'. A purported juvenile carcass extracted in October 1937 from the stomach of a sperm whale processed at the Naden Harbour whaling station was photographed and tentatively examined before being lost; cetologists today usually attribute it to a known animal (most plausibly a fetal baleen whale or basking shark). Carcasses subsequently associated with Caddy have all been identified as known species (basking sharks, decomposed whales, oarfish, elephant seals). Indigenous Pacific Northwest Coast peoples maintain long-standing traditions of large sea creatures — including the Manhousat hiyitlik and the Kwakwaka'wakw sisiutl — that predate and remain conceptually distinct from the colonial-era Cadborosaurus framing. Cetacean biologists Edward L. Bousfield and Paul LeBlond compiled approximately 200 sightings and proposed the binomial 'Cadborosaurus willsi' in a 1995 paper, an attribution rejected by the mainstream zoological community. Skeptics, including Darren Naish, argue that the sightings record is best explained by a heterogeneous mix of misidentified known species rather than a single unknown animal.

etymology.origin: Coined by Archie Wills, managing editor of the Victoria Daily Times, in late 1933 following Major W. H. Langley's sighting near Discovery Island. Constructed from 'Cadboro' (Cadboro Bay, Victoria, B.C.) plus the Greek 'sauros' (lizard).
etymology.meaning: 'Cadboro Bay lizard' — applied by analogy with classical-zoology naming.

features.description: Witnesses repeatedly describe a long, flexible neck capable of being held vertically above the water
Small head with prominent eyes; sometimes mane-like growth at the back
Dorsal humps that break the water sequentially, sometimes interpreted as vertical undulations
Pair of pectoral flippers reported in many accounts
Posterior fluke described in Bousfield/LeBlond's reconstruction
Langley's 1933 description noted serrated marks along the back and sides

physical.morphology: Bousfield and LeBlond (1995) reconstructed Cadborosaurus as a marine reptile-like animal with a long neck, vertical undulation, paired flippers, and a fan-shaped tail. Mainstream cetologists treat this reconstruction as an artifact of pooling diverse misidentified animals.

abilities.description: Witnesses describe high apparent speeds, in some accounts faster than nearby boats
Reportedly moves with vertical (rather than horizontal) body waves, unlike known fish
Disappears beneath the surface when noticed by witnesses

behavior.diet: Hypothesised piscivorous in pro-cryptid accounts; no direct evidence.
patterns: Sighting reports peak in late summer when boating activity is highest
Concentrated in inland B.C. waters but extending from Alaska to California
Sightings frequently associated with salmon runs

range.description: The reported range covers the Pacific coast from Alaska to northern California, with the densest cluster of sightings in the inland waters around Vancouver Island, the Strait of Georgia, Puget Sound, and adjacent inlets.

origins.cultural_roots: Indigenous Pacific Northwest Coast traditions of large sea beings, including the Manhousat hiyitlik and Kwakwaka'wakw sisiutl, predate the colonial-era cryptid framing.
origins.earliest_accounts: Indigenous oral tradition; first published English-language sighting reports from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a global family of long-necked sea-serpent traditions, and within North America to Ogopogo and Champ.

timeline.event: Major W. H. Langley reports a sighting near Discovery Island; the Victoria Daily Times publishes the account, and editor Archie Wills coins 'Cadborosaurus'
A purported juvenile Caddy carcass is recovered from the stomach of a sperm whale at the Naden Harbour whaling station
timeline.significance: Most-cited physical-evidence claim; specimen subsequently lost
timeline.source: Naden Harbour whaling station records; Bousfield & LeBlond (1995)

timeline.source: Bousfield, E. L. & LeBlond, P. H. (1995), Amphipacifica

timeline.event: Alaskan fisherman Kelly Nash claims to have filmed multiple Cadborosaurus-type animals in Nushagak Bay

history.modern_era: Cadborosaurus continues to draw periodic media attention from fishing communities along the British Columbia and Alaska coasts. The mainstream zoological consensus is that the case rests on an aggregation of misidentified known species — most prominently basking sharks, oarfish, decomposed whales, sea lions in line formation, and elephant seals — and that the physical-evidence record contains no specimen verifiable as a new taxon. The 1995 'Cadborosaurus willsi' proposal has been criticised by zoologists including Darren Naish for relying on heterogeneous eyewitness accounts and a single lost photograph.

notable.name: Major W. H. Langley sighting (Discovery Island)

location.description: Inshore waters near Discovery Island, off Cadboro Bay

types: Major W. H. Langley (clerk of the B.C. Legislature)

notable.description: Langley and his wife, sailing near Discovery Island, reported seeing the dome of a creature's back break the surface within roughly 30 m (100 ft) of their boat. The animal was described as the size of a large whale but unlike any known species, dark greenish-brown, with serrated marks along its back and sides. The Victoria Daily Times published the account under managing editor Archie Wills, who coined the name 'Cadborosaurus'.
evidence: Newspaper coverage in the Victoria Daily Times

credibility.notes: Foundational modern Caddy report; the basis for the name.

sources: Bousfield, E. L. & LeBlond, P. H. (1995)

notable.name: Naden Harbour carcass

location.description: Naden Harbour whaling station, Haida Gwaii

notable.description: A roughly 3 m (10 ft) carcass with a long neck, horse-like head, and serpentine body was recovered from the stomach of a sperm whale processed at the Naden Harbour whaling station. The remains were photographed before being shipped to the Pacific Biological Station at Nanaimo for identification, and were subsequently lost.
evidence: Photograph of the carcass on a wooden plank

factors: Most plausibly a fetal baleen whale or basking shark
credibility.notes: Most-cited physical-evidence case; mainstream zoologists view it as a misidentified known species.

sources: Bousfield, E. L. & LeBlond, P. H. (1995)

physical.name: Naden Harbour carcass
physical.description: Long-necked carcass recovered from the stomach of a sperm whale at Naden Harbour, photographed and then lost.
physical.location: Naden Harbour whaling station, Haida Gwaii, B.C.
physical.analysis: Mainstream zoologists most often interpret it as a fetal baleen whale or basking shark; cryptozoologists Bousfield and LeBlond (1995) argue for a juvenile Cadborosaurus.
physical.source: Bousfield, E. L. & LeBlond, P. H. (1995)

photographic.name: Naden Harbour carcass photograph
photographic.description: Photograph of the 1937 Naden Harbour carcass on a wooden plank.
photographic.analysis: The image is real but the subject is contested; identification as a known animal is favoured by mainstream zoologists.
photographic.source: Naden Harbour whaling station; reproduced in Bousfield & LeBlond (1995)

video.name: Kelly Nash Nushagak Bay footage
video.description: Video footage shot by Alaskan fisherman Kelly Nash purportedly showing several Cadborosaurus-type animals.
video.analysis: Image quality and animal identifications are contested; mainstream interpreters favour known marine mammals.

documentary.analysis: Most-cited academic argument for Caddy as an unknown species; rejected by mainstream zoology.
documentary.source: Bousfield, E. L. & LeBlond, P. H. (1995), Amphipacifica

scientific.name: Undescribed long-necked marine animal
scientific.description: Bousfield and LeBlond argue that the consistent long-necked, vertically-undulating profile across many independent witnesses points to an undescribed marine reptile or mammal.
evidence_cited: Indigenous traditions of large sea creatures

skeptical.name: Misidentification of basking shark and other large fish
skeptical.description: Many long-bodied surface sightings are best explained by basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus), which can exceed 9 m (30 ft) and produce 'humped' wakes when surface-feeding.
evidence_cited: Basking shark distribution in Pacific Northwest waters

skeptical.name: Decomposed whale or oarfish carcasses
skeptical.description: The 1937 Naden Harbour carcass and similar specimens are best explained by fetal baleen whales, partially-decomposed cetaceans, or oarfish (Regalecus glesne).
proponents: Cetologists at Pacific Biological Station, Nanaimo

skeptical.name: Aggregated heterogeneous misidentifications
skeptical.description: Naish argues that the case is best explained by treating Caddy not as a single creature but as a category that pools different misidentified animals (sea lions in formation, elephant seals, basking sharks) under one cultural label.
evidence_cited: 1943 Georgia Strait police-report case later identified as sea lions in formation

traditions: Pacific Northwest Coast First Nations traditions of large sea beings
stories: 1933 Langley Discovery Island sighting and naming of Caddy
folklore.beliefs: Caddy occupies a comfortable place in regional Pacific Northwest folklore; he is a tourist mascot, an object of serious cryptozoological investigation, and a continuing subject of newspaper interest.

indigenous.significance: Pacific Northwest Coast peoples maintain long-running traditions of large sea creatures with their own names and ceremonial significance.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: First Nations traditions about sea beings are not interchangeable with the colonial 'Caddy' framing and should be cited with care.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Engage relevant First Nations cultural authorities for any region-specific use of these traditions; cite Indigenous knowledge holders directly.
